candidates.attacker_control: Any URI consumed by the library on behalf of an untrusted party: e.g. HttpGet/RequestBuilder URI strings (CloseableHttpClient.execute(HttpUriRequest) → determineTarget) or an HTTP response's `Location` header (DefaultRedirectStrategy.createLocationURI → RedirectExec → extractHost) for redirect-enabled clients. The attacker controls the full authority text.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The fallback is deliberate compatibility logic, not dead code: existing tests require extractHost to return HttpHost for authorities the JDK parser rejects, e.g. `http://local_host/` (TestURIUtils.java:228-231) and `http://localhost:8080;sessionid=stuff/abcd` (TestURIUtils.java:257-262), so a fix cannot simply delete the fallback. HttpHost construction is wrapped in try/catch (URIUtils.java:380-383) and rejects blank/whitespace hostnames, so several malformed authorities still yield null (e.g. `http://:80/robots.txt`, `http://some%20domain:80/robots.txt` — TestURIUtils.java:263-266), and for ordinary userinfo-before-host forms the heuristic coincides with RFC parsing. The exact runtime behavior of java.net.URI.getHost()/getAuthority() and of HttpHost's validation could not be executed or read (HttpHost lives in the httpcore artifact, not in this snapshot), so the concrete SSRF example is analytical, not reproduced. The known public advisory for this code path (CVE-2020-13956, fixed after 4.5.12) matches the mechanism but its fix diff was not inspectable in this run.
candidates.impact: The client can be induced to send requests to a host that its own URI parser reported as invalid/absent (host confusion). For applications that validate the endpoint with URI.getHost()/uri.getAuthority() (SSRF allowlists, scheme+host checks) this can bypass validation and reach internal services or cloud metadata endpoints, and it also skews origin-scoped state (cookies are matched against clientContext.getTargetHost() in RequestAddCookies.java:104-146; preemptive credentials are selected by target host in RequestAuthCache/MainClientExec). Severity depends on the caller, but the primitive is exactly the 'malformed authority → wrong target host for request execution' class described for this component.
candidates.prerequisites: Client built from HttpClients.createDefault()/HttpClientBuilder (extractHost is on the default code path); for the redirect variant, redirects must be enabled (default) and the malicious Location must come from a server the client talks to; for the direct variant, the application must pass a malformed-authority URL through (typically because its own validation relies on URI.getHost(), which is null for such URIs, or on string checks that see a different host). A malformed authority whose remainder (after '@'/' :' heuristics) is a valid, resolvable hostname/address is required.
candidates.root_cause: When java.net.URI.getHost() returns null because the authority cannot be parsed as a valid host, URIUtils.extractHost does not reject the URI: it falls back to manually splitting the *decoded* authority returned by uri.getAuthority() (strip at the first '@', split at the first ':', consume leading digits as port) and then constructs `new HttpHost(host, port, scheme)` from the unvalidated remainder (URIUtils.java:341-384). The only validation applied is a blank check plus whatever HttpHost enforces (blank/whitespace), so a host string that the URI parser itself rejected is accepted and used to plan the route/connection. The chosen host can therefore differ from what the URI 'means' per RFC 3986 and from what the calling application validated via URI.getHost().
candidates.title: URIUtils.extractHost derives an attacker-influenced target host from a malformed URI authority (wrong-host / SSRF-style host confusion)
candidates.trace: Direct: HttpGet("http://evil.com:80;@169.254.169.254/") → CloseableHttpClient.execute(HttpUriRequest) → determineTarget (CloseableHttpClient.java:91-98) → URIUtils.extractHost (URIUtils.java:340-384): URI.getHost()==null (port "80;" is not a valid port, so the authority is not server-parseable) → host = getAuthority() = "evil.com:80;@169.254.169.254" → strip at first '@' → host "169.254.169.254" → `new HttpHost("169.254.169.254", -1, "http")` succeeds → route planner connects to 169.254.169.254:80; ProtocolExec rewrites the absolute URI to a relative one (URIUtils.java:208-228), so the socket destination and the request line/Host header are both derived from the guessed host. Redirect variant: server returns `Location: http://evil.com:80;@169.254.169.254/` → DefaultRedirectStrategy.createLocationURI accepts it (URIBuilder preserves the raw authority, URIBuilder.java:126-146) → RedirectExec.java:134-139 calls extractHost, gets 169.254.169.254, resets auth state because the target changed, and plans a new route to that host.
candidates.unverified: No execution or runtime reproduction; the worked example (`http://evil.com:80;@169.254.169.254/`) depends on JDK URI parsing details that were inferred from source/javadoc rather than observed, and on HttpHost (external httpcore) accepting the resulting host string. Whether the dataset's ground-truth issue is exactly this code path is not established; alternatively it could be a variant involving percent-encoded or duplicate-'@' authorities. No exploit payload or reproduction steps are provided.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-20 improper input validation (malformed URI authority) leading to wrong target-host selection (CWE-918 SSRF / host confusion)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 796 files at the assigned root, 795 model-visible after the sensitive-path/name filter (1 excluded); binary-like files are skipped. P1 relation index: 795 files, 760 Java files parsed, 11 files omitted (index_status=partial), 9,015 symbols, 23,460 syntax edges, 40,222 call sites with 27,505 unresolved; control-flow and data-flow are not implemented and semantic/Spring enforcement is unverified, so index edges were used only for navigation and all claims were re-checked in source text. Audit coverage focused on the non-deprecated httpclient module (client/utils URIUtils/URIBuilder/URLEncodedUtils, client/protocol interceptors, client/methods/RequestBuilder, impl/client incl. HttpClientBuilder and cookie specs, impl/execchain, impl/conn route planners/connection manager, impl/auth, conn/ssl verifiers and SSLConnectionSocketFactory, conn/util PublicSuffix*), the httpclient-cache main sources (CachingExec, CacheKeyGenerator, ResponseCachingPolicy, FileResourceFactory, serializers), httpmime, fluent-hc, httpclient-win, plus poms/RELEASE_NOTES/BUILDING. Partially reviewed: large files (NTLMEngineImpl ~67 KB, deprecated DefaultRequestDirector ~49 KB, cache protocol test suites) and most java-deprecated classes; the huge cache test corpus and examples were only sampled.
limitations: No code execution, tests, scanners or exploit payloads were run (per task rules); all conclusions are static and the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

The httpcore dependency (HttpHost, header parsers, connection classes) is not part of this snapshot, so its validation semantics (e.g. Args.containsNoBlanks) and the exact behavior of java.net.URI on percent-encoded/malformed authorities could only be inferred, not verified.

No git history, fix commit, patch, CVE/CWE database or external service was consulted; the mapping of this snapshot to the dataset's ground-truth issue is inferred from the source and the component's known advisory history.
The P1 index is partial: 11 omitted files, no data/control flow, many unresolved calls; unreported areas were not treated as reviewed.

Large security-adjacent files were not read line-by-line (NTLMEngineImpl, deprecated request director/SSL factory, most cache protocol tests, parts of HttpClientBuilder beyond the build() pipeline), so additional issues in those areas cannot be excluded.

The concrete malformed-authority string used in the trace was derived analytically; a different variant (percent-encoding, duplicate '@') may be needed to reproduce on a given JDK, and the practical exploitability depends on the embedding application's own URI validation.

rejected_leads.lead: AbstractVerifier.getDNSSubjectAlts inverted ternary (httpclient/src/main/java/org/apache/http/conn/ssl/AbstractVerifier.java:270 returns an empty array when SANs exist and null when they do not, contradicting its javadoc).
rejected_leads.reason: Bug is real and source-verifiable, but the method is a deprecated public utility with no in-repo callers, so no attacker-controlled path or impact could be demonstrated; cannot be called a vulnerability from source evidence alone.

rejected_leads.lead: NetscapeDomainHandler.match uses host.endsWith(domain) without a dot boundary (NetscapeDomainHandler.java:110-119), so domain "example.com" matches "notexample.com".
rejected_leads.reason: Only reachable when the deprecated 'netscape' cookie policy is explicitly selected; the default policy (DefaultCookieSpec, DefaultCookieSpec.java:89-95) wires BasicDomainHandler, which enforces the dot boundary. Non-default configuration + no in-repo attacker path reduces it to a hardening lead.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultHostnameVerifier.matchIdentity strict remainder substring can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException for overlapping wildcard prefix/suffix (DefaultHostnameVerifier.java:225-229); AbstractVerifier.matchIdentity has a similar host.substring prefix issue (AbstractVerifier.java:211).
rejected_leads.reason: Unchecked exception on crafted certificate SANs appears to fail the TLS handshake (fail-closed) rather than bypass verification; DoS/robustness at most, and no counterexample of a bypass was found.

rejected_leads.lead: MultipartEntityBuilder.generateBoundary uses new java.util.Random() (httpmime MultipartEntityBuilder.java:191-199), giving a non-cryptographic MIME boundary.
rejected_leads.reason: Boundary is not attacker-observable/controllable in the normal flow and matches upstream behavior; exploitation would require the application to splice attacker content into the multipart body, which is caller misuse.

rejected_leads.lead: ServiceUnavailableRetryExec retries without checking idempotency or request repeatability (ServiceUnavailableRetryExec.java:83-108), and RedirectExec copies all original request headers into redirect requests (RedirectExec.java:122-128).
rejected_leads.reason: Both match the modern upstream implementation and depend on user-provided strategies/headers; no evidence of a defect introduced in this revision.

rejected_leads.lead: Redirected/originating Host and target-host derivations in ProtocolExec/MainClientExec could disagree when an explicit HttpHost target is passed together with an absolute URI.
rejected_leads.reason: Behavior is by design for proxy-style usage; no source-verifiable security defect could be established.

summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot of Apache HttpComponents Client 4.5.3-SNAPSHOT (repo-root pom.xml:36, branch 4.5.x) as a defensive source-code assessment, using the P1 relation index for navigation and verifying every candidate in source. The snapshot covers the client, cache, mime, fluent, osgi and win modules (795 model-visible files; 760 Java files parsed by the index, 11 omitted). I traced the strongest plausible issue to the URI-authority → target-host derivation in `org.apache.http.client.utils.URIUtils#extractHost`, which is on the default request path (`CloseableHttpClient.determineTarget`) and on the redirect path (`RedirectExec`). The candidate is submitted as a lead only; no runtime testing, scanner, diff or CVE database was consulted, so it is not runtime-confirmed and its mapping to the dataset ground truth is unproven.
